title: Smishing: the package that never came
brief: 17:25. A text from Dropwell Couriers: a parcel is held at the depot, and a small fee will release it.
insight: Texts have no spam filter worth the name, and a sender name like DROPWELL costs nothing to fake.
teaches: Read the link, not the panic: check where a text's link really goes
Go to the courier's real site yourself to track a parcel
Never pay a “release fee” from a text: the fee is small because the card details are the prize

/.warn: Pay within 12 hours or your parcel will be returned to the sender.

kv: No parcel found with this number

/.note: Dropwell never charges a redelivery fee by text, and we will never text you a link to pay.

/.p: Missed a delivery? We leave a card with a reference, and rebooking is free.

value.title: Dropwell Couriers: track a parcel
value.text: Official Dropwell tracking. Enter your reference to see where your parcel is.

from.name: DROPWELL
details: Shown as DROPWELL, but a text can show any name it likes. The number behind it is an ordinary mobile.

messages.text: Dropwell: your parcel DW-{{ref}} could not be delivered. A {{fee}} redelivery fee is due within 12 hours or it will be returned to the sender.

outcome.label: Checked who really sent the text
outcome.what: The name says DROPWELL. The number is an ordinary mobile.
outcome.ideal: checks the number behind a sender name.

outcome.label: Checked where the link goes
outcome.what: The link goes to {{host}}. Dropwell's real site is dropwell.co.uk.
outcome.ideal: reads a text's link before tapping it.

outcome.label: Tracked it on Dropwell's real site
outcome.what: No parcel exists with that number, and Dropwell never charges fees by text.
outcome.ideal: goes to the courier's real site instead of the link in the text.

outcome.label: Opened the link in the text
outcome.what: It opened {{host}}. Nothing is lost yet, but that page exists to collect card details.
outcome.ideal: checks the link before tapping it.

decide.objective: Decide what to do about the Dropwell text.
decide.insight: The fee is tiny on purpose. Nobody thinks twice about £1.99. What they want is the card number, the expiry and the security code.

hint.text: Open the text, check the sender's number and tap “Where does this link go?”. Search Seekly for Dropwell to track the parcel on their real site. Then report the text.

outcome.label: Paid the release fee
outcome.what: Your full card details went to the attacker for {{fee}}. Expect the card to be used within hours, and a follow up call from “your bank” offering to help.
outcome.ideal: never pays a fee from a text, and tracks parcels on the courier's own site.

card.title: {{fee}} for your card details
body: There was no parcel. The page on {{host}} took the card number, expiry and security code, which is everything needed to spend on your card.
Dropwell's real tracking page, one search away, would have shown no parcel and a note that they never charge by text. Call your bank on the number on the back of the card and cancel it.
card.ideal: reads the link, not the panic, and goes to the courier's real site.

outcome.label: Reported the text as spam
outcome.what: Reporting a scam text helps the mobile networks block the number and the link for everyone.
outcome.ideal: reports scam texts rather than just deleting them.

card.title: No parcel, no fee, reported
body: You reported the text instead of paying. The link went to {{host}}, not dropwell.co.uk.
Texts arrive with none of the checks email gets. The defence is the same: the real address, and the real site you find yourself.
card.ideal: checks the link and the sender, then reports.

outcome.label: Blocked or deleted the text
outcome.what: Safe for you. Reporting it as well helps block it for everyone else.
outcome.ideal: reports scam texts, so the number and link get blocked.

auto.text: Report the text, and tell the service desk your card was taken.

hint.text: Report the text as spam, or raise a Helpdesk ticket.
